title: Caring for the sick
tomorrow: Abuela never talks about the baby before Tomás. why now?

cards: Someone in your life is doing it this week. Maybe it's you. Driving to every appointment.
Learning the names of the medicines. Sleeping badly in a chair by a bed, then answering, I'm fine, whenever anyone asks. Who takes care of the person taking care of everyone?
The Gospels have a man who got pulled into that job without warning, on the road to the cross.

teach.b: Luke says that as they led Jesus away, the soldiers laid hold of a man named Simon of Cyrene, coming in from the country, and laid the cross on him to carry behind Jesus. Simon didn't volunteer. He was walking into town.
Suddenly he's carrying weight that isn't his, right behind the one who's suffering.
One to tell a friend: Mark even names Simon's sons, Alexander and Rufus, as if he expected readers to know the family.
Catholics pray this moment in the Stations of the Cross, and it fits every caregiver: a cross carried behind someone else's, which nobody in the crowd is looking at. That's the hidden cross.

Jesus said where to look, in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "sick, and you visited me." The Church counts visiting the sick among the works of mercy. But the visitor and the caregiver get tired too.
So the answer to today's question is the rest of us. A meal on the step. A drive to the clinic.
An hour on a Saturday so they can sleep.
The Gospels give Simon no lines at all, only the weight.

how: Catholics count visiting the sick among the corporal works of mercy; parishes may organize meals, rides and visits for the sick and their caregivers, and some bring them Communion at home.

games.q: what does “caring for the sick” mean?
o: the daily, unseen work of looking after someone ill
a special blessing given only by a priest
a hospital's work, left to doctors and nurses

games.q: the road to the cross — tap the pairs.

s: Simon of Cyrene volunteered to carry the cross
the soldiers laid hold of him as he came in from the country. it landed on him.
Jesus says visiting the sick is visiting him
sick, and you visited me: Matthew 25.
if the patient is getting good care, the caregiver needs nothing
the caregiver's cross is the hidden one; the rest of us are their Simon.

games.q: your neighbor has looked after her husband since his stroke. at church people always ask how he's doing. what fits today?
o: ask how she's doing, and offer one specific thing, like Thursday's dinner.
keep asking about him; that's what she'd want people to focus on.
leave her alone so she can save her energy for him.
games.why: the caregiver carries a hidden cross. Simon carried weight behind someone else's suffering; she needs a Simon too.

practice: Count, on your fingers, the people who have cared for you when you were sick: a parent, a nurse, a friend with soup. Fold a finger down for each name. Then bring to mind one person caring for someone right now, and hold them there.
If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Caring for the sick. The daily, unseen work of looking after someone who's ill, and a cross this tradition says should be shared. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: to visit the sick, one of the corporal works of mercy.

carryVoice: Your line: the hidden cross, carried right behind someone else's, where nobody looks. Day done.

sources.ref: Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (the works of mercy)
Stations of the Cross, fifth station (Simon of Cyrene helps Jesus carry the cross)
